Q: Can I defer the execution of a pipeline assignment A:

I don't think there is a clean workaround to this other than offering the consumer to decide what they want to do via switch parameter to output the IEnumerator / IEnumerable optionally when present:

function New-Range {
    param(
        [int] $Start = 0,
        [int] $Count = 10,
        [switch] $AsEnumerable)

    $ienumerable = [System.Linq.Enumerable]::Select(
        [System.Linq.Enumerable]::Range($Start, $Count),
        [System.Func[int, int]] { Start-Sleep 1; $args[0] })

    if ($AsEnumerable) { return , $ienumerable }
    $ienumerable
}

# streams output, takes 10 seconds
New-Range | ForEach-Object { "[$_]" }

# deferred execution, takes no time
$ienumerable = New-Range -AsEnumerable
# takes 10 seconds when enumerating it
$ienumerable | ForEach-Object { "[$_]" }

Q: eBPF as non-root can't freeze map .rodata when trying to make a hello world program A:

There are several ways to create the constant string "My Hello world!\n" in BPF and it seems your loader is choosing to use a frozen map to hold the string. That can probably be worked around as I've seen bcc use a simple literal to hold strings instead of a map.

However, bpf_printk is not available without elevated privileges. So even if you could avoid the map for the constant string, you still wouldn't be able to load this program without privileges.

Specifically, bpf_printk requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN or CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON: https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v6.7-rc8/source/kernel/bpf/helpers.c#L1792.

In general, unprivileged BPF programs are very limited. As you've noticed, few program types are available, but also few helpers, and the verifier imposes various stricter limits (ex. program size, program complexity, speculative execution).

Q: How to get payload data from tcp_probe tracepoint via ebpf? A:

TL;DR. Your code is probably not showing anything because the syntax %.*s isn't supported by the bpf_trace_printk helper.

Sources

From the documentation:

The conversion specifiers supported by fmt are similar, but more limited than for printk(). They are %d, %i, %u, %x, %ld, %li, %lu, %lx, %lld, %lli, %llu, %llx, %p, %s. No modifier (size of field, padding with zeroes, etc.) is available, and the helper will return -EINVAL (but print nothing) if it encounters an unknown specifier.

Testing

If I run the following program with bcc:

char payload[10] = "Tail-call";
int res = bpf_trace_printk("PAYLOAD: %.*s", payload);
if (res < 0) {
    bpf_trace_printk("The first call to bpf_trace_printk failed.");
}
return 0;

Then bcc warns me about my incorrect specifier and the first printk call then fails:

$ sudo python3 examples/hello_world.py 
/virtual/main.c:4:42: warning: only %d %u %x %ld %lu %lx %lld %llu %llx %p %s conversion specifiers allowed
    int res = bpf_trace_printk("PAYLOAD: %.*s", payload);
                                         ^
1 warning generated.
b' gnome-terminal--7331    [003] ...21  1095.386386: bpf_trace_printk: The first call to bpf_trace_printk failed.'
b' gnome-terminal--7896    [004] ...21  1095.395751: bpf_trace_printk: The first call to bpf_trace_printk failed.'
b'            bash-7898    [002] ...21  1095.396742: bpf_trace_printk: The first call to bpf_trace_printk failed.'
